items.originalTitle: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.author: Meredith Lee Hill
items.title: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno isn’t sugarcoating things. The incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee will be in charge of defending 19 GOP seats in 2028 — and he’ll need to flip at least six more to regain control of the Senate majority. “Looking at it right now, it's absolutely a savagely brutal map,” the Ohio Republican said in an interview on Capitol Hill. After a historic midterms shellacking, Moreno is in the hot seat as he looks to navigate his chamber — and the party — through a rebuilding of its brand and its base over next two years. Republicans will likely have just 44 seats heading into 2028. They need to hold onto seats in battleground states like Wisconsin and North Carolina, while trying to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly in Arizona, John Fetterman in Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock in Georgia and Catherine Cortez Masto in Nevada. Moreno and his team have interviewed a handful of candidates over the last few days to be the next NRSC executive director, according to four people with direct knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. Republicans expect Chris Grant, a former Moreno and Trump campaign staffer who now runs his own firm, to serve as a main outside GOP consultant for the committee. On top of the grueling map ahead, the Ohio Republican is facing the additional task of working with a lame duck president who still wields immense power over the GOP and its primaries. Then there’s the vice president, who is likely to run for president himself in the same two-year sprint. Moreno is close with both of those men. Asked how involved he expects the White House to be in GOP primaries and recruiting going forward, he replied, “We’re going to work on all of that.” It’ll be a complicated path forward. Moreno, over the past cycle has been unwilling to cast blame on President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance. Days before the midterm elections, he said if Republicans lost, it would be because people were “pissed off” about high gas prices. He’s unlikely to completely distance himself and the NRSC brand from the president's influence. But the party is currently undergoing a reckoning of how closely to align with the president after voters delivered an uncompromising rebuke of Trump’s economic agenda. Across the country, several battlegrounds and once-thought-to-be-safe red territory fell to Democratic hands. Trump in the 2026 cycle angered many Senate Republicans by supporting a primary challenge against Sen. John Cornyn of Texas — a move they privately say cost them north of $200 million as they tried, in vain, to save Ken Paxton’s imperiled campaign. The president also supported a primary challenge against Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, and pushed Sen. Thom Tillis to decide to retire in highly competitive North Carolina. One of the biggest challenges before Moreno and Senate Republicans after the midterms wipeout is to find candidates who can win a general election in highly competitive states, while also making it through GOP primaries where Trump will be a major factor. They’ll need to push back on the White House if the president tries, once again, to intervene — though that’s easier said than done. “There will be no patience for bad recruits this cycle,” said one senior Republican granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations, referring to the implosions of Paxton, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and other Republicans who were hand-picked by Trump. The White House referred POLITICO to Trump's post-midterms comments, where he blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot and said he brought several candidates "closer to victory," though they ultimately lost. Senate Majority Leader John Thune — who will be the minority leader next year — and his team plan to be heavily involved in recruitment efforts, according to two people involved in the conversations, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Their goal, one of the people said, is “to make sure we have our strongest possible candidates on the ballot in 2028.” Moreno is already trying to find a GOP recruit in his home state of Ohio to run against incoming Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, whose term will be up again in 2028 after he won a special election against GOP Sen. Jon Husted earlier this month. The new NRSC chair said he’s looking for “somebody who can beat the crap out of Sherrod Brown.” Husted in private conversations hasn’t completely ruled out another bid, but he’s indicated he’s unlikely to run again, according to three people with knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Ohio Republicans expect former state Sen. Kevin Coughlin to explore a potential Senate bid. And they’re watching Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), who just lost his reelection. Husted did not respond to a request for comment. A Turner spokesperson said in a statement that the representative "has been approached by several people about this and is keeping all his options open.” If Vance doesn’t seek his own presidential bid, Republicans in his home state are holding a long-shot hope that he, too, might consider a return to his old job. “JD Vance would be a dream candidate,” said one Ohio Republican. A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score . Want to receive the newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro . You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.

items.originalTitle: Poll: Most Americans think a Democrat will be the next president
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.title: Poll: Most Americans think a Democrat will be the next president
items.summary: Nearly twice as many Americans expect a Democrat to win the presidency in 2028 than they do a Republican, a new POLITICO Poll finds . Even one in five of President Donald Trump’s own 2024 voters believe Republicans will lose the White House, a bad sign for the GOP as it struggles to recover from widespread losses this cycle and figure out its identity after spending a decade orbiting around Trump. Just 60% of Trump voters believe Republicans will keep the White House. Democratic voters are far more confident about their own party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global in the days after the midterm: Among voters who backed Kamala Harris, 87% expect Democrats to win in 2028. Beneath the unity is disagreement over what kind of nominee to pick. Pluralities of voters agree the next president should be a fighter when asked to choose from a list of qualities. But voters across the ideological spectrum also said they want other things from the country’s 48th president. While 43% of Harris voters want “a fighter,” 40% also selected “a progressive” and 34% chose “creative.” Among Trump voters, the 45% said they want to see “a conservative” elected president, surpassing the 39% who picked “a fighter.” They're also divided over what background their nominees should come from. Nearly three in 10 Trump voters say they would prefer the next president be someone who has not worked in Trump’s administration. That number rises to 46% among Trump voters who don’t identify as MAGA, whereas 82% of his loyal MAGA base would prefer the next president be someone who did work for Trump. That debate is playing out in real-time among top GOP leaders and lawmakers. More and more Hill Republicans are eyeing Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 2028, who they say is less associated with the midterm bloodbath than Vice President JD Vance. Others say the nominee should be someone entirely outside of Trump’s direct orbit. “As much as I like Rubio, and as much as I like Vance, they can't be our nominee,” said Dan McMaster, the chair of Michigan’s Shiawassee County Republican Party. “We need to get a Republican as far away from Trump as possible, and even then, I think it's going to be a battle.” “You've got to have some fresh blood in there, and you've got to have someone that has some distance from the crap that's gone on the last two years,” said one GOP strategist who worked on multiple House races last cycle and was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party. In a statement, Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said the president isn’t going anywhere. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs, and secured our border,” Baldassarre said. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028." The White House also pointed POLITICO to separate polling earlier this month that shows Trump’s approval rating sits at 75% with all Republicans and jumps to 93% with those who identify as MAGA. “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson. On election night earlier this month, Trump blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot, telling POLITICO by phone , “I wasn't on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, we would have won; we would have won it all very easily.” Meanwhile, Democrats have their own disagreements to figure out as they select their nominee. This cycle’s blue wave has bolstered the progressive wing of the party, which has long hoped to prove their candidates can win in purple battlegrounds, not just in safe-blue states. But the poll reveals skepticism remains — at least among moderates — over whether progressive wins in 2026 can translate to the presidential stage in 2028. The survey found a majority of progressive Democrats — 63% — want a progressive to be president, compared with just 23% of moderates who say the same. Half of progressive Democrats are convinced that being a progressive is a quality that will get their candidate elected in 2028. Moderates are less certain of that, though they’re also not as confident in their own faction: Just 37% think being a moderate is a quality that ensures the Democratic candidate wins. “Whoever's running for president has seen what's happened and also has seen the power of our movement, and so this is something that could be carried on to 2028,” said progressive New Jersey Democratic Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, reflecting on the wins he and others enjoyed this cycle. “Despite it being the most expensive elections in history, we showed that people are able to beat out money when we come together.” And with Democrats winning Senate seats in deep-red states like Kansas and Mississippi for the first time in decades, many now argue that the entire map is in play for 2028. The poll found that 60% of Democrats think the party should focus their efforts on winning all states in the presidential election, even ones that seemed like deep Republican areas, rather than focus on holding the states where they know their supporters are. Republicans felt the same, with 56% also arguing for an “all states” approach as the party races to rebuild in territory they once thought was safe. “I have been very, very loud about the fact that the path to the presidency leads through the South,” said Democratic strategist Dallas Jones, who ran statewide Black voter engagement for Lone Star Rising PAC, the outside group that supported Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. “But again, we don't make investments there. We're playing the same electoral map with the same swing states.”

items.originalTitle: How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share
items.author: Cameron Faulkner
items.title: How The Verge is picking which Black Friday deals to share
items.summary: For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands big and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them. Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them. Something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case. In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow , an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon. View this post on Instagram The group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care. Vetting deals for coverage consideration is a big, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors. With Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover. We follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass For products hit by recent price hikes, the new deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example. To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. ( You can use them, too! ) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool , which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass. We cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge . However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

Her win gives Democrats a 56-44 edge in the Senate. Peltola was one of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s top recruits for the cycle. She overpowered a Republican rescue mission for Sullivan and allegations of misconduct against her from former staffers to flip a state President Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Her victory continues the blue wave born from voters’ frustrations at high costs and the Trump administration. Peltola will return to Washington, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate after previously holding the same distinction in the House. Her campaign had projected confidence about her path to victory as the vote count dragged on in a far-flung, rural state with long grace periods for late-arriving ballots. But her win was not without tumult. Trump’s Department of Justice sued to try to stop the certification if Sullivan lost, claiming voters could be confused by his same-name challenger. The president went so far as to call for votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and another longshot candidate in the four-way, all-party contest to be transferred to the incumbent. The Justice Department also started probing efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan after a New York Times report suggesting members of Peltola’s campaign and Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were involved. items.originalTitle: How TIME and Statista Determined America's Top Manufacturers of 2027
items.author: Olivia B. Waxman
items.title: How TIME and Statista Determined America's Top Manufacturers of 2027
items.summary: —Illustration by TIME; Filo—Getty Images For the first edition of America’s Top Manufacturers , TIME and Statista have joined forces to recognize 250 leading U.S. manufacturers. As companies navigate shifting supply chains and evolving workforce demands, the ranking highlights performance across three equally weighted dimensions: financial performance, innovation capacity, and employment. Methodology The selection process began with U.S.-based companies classified in manufacturing under North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes 31–33. To qualify, companies needed at least $100 million in 2025 revenue and production facilities in the United States. The methodology then evaluated eligible companies using company disclosures, public databases, patent analytics, and targeted research. ● Financial performance: Companies were assessed on revenue growth and changes in net income from 2023 to 2025, as well as their 2025 net profit margin and the ratio of capital expenditure (CapEx) to revenue. Changes in CapEx over the same period were also considered. Financial information was drawn from companies’ 10-K filings. ● Innovation capacity: This dimension measured both investment in research and development (R&D) and the strength of companies’ patent portfolios. It considered R&D expenditure as a share of revenue, changes in R&D expenditure from 2023 to 2025, and the Patent Asset Index. Patent data was provided by LexisNexis® Intellectual Property Solutions through its PatentSight+™ analytics platform. ● Employment: The employment assessment covered productivity, workforce growth, retention, and workplace safety. It compared 2025 revenue per full time equivalent (FTE) with the industry median and assessed U.S. workforce growth and voluntary and overall employee turnover. Workplace safety was measured using TRIR¹ and either LTIR² or DART³, each compared with its respective industry median. Where applicable, employment KPIs also captured changes from 2023 to 2025. Companies with no work-related fatalities from 2021 through 2025 received points. Data came from companies’ Form 10-K filings, ESG/CSR reports, and the OSHA⁴ database. The indicators were consolidated into a scoring model, with each of the three dimensions contributing one-third of the overall result. Companies received a final score on a scale of 1 to 100 points. The 250 highest-performing eligible companies were recognized as America’s Top Manufacturers 2027 . See the full list here.

items.originalTitle: How TIME and Statista Determined the World's Best Airports of 2027
items.author: TIME Staff
items.title: How TIME and Statista Determined the World's Best Airports of 2027
items.summary: —Getty Images/John Seaton Callahan The “World’s Best Airports” list is a comprehensive evaluation, conducted by Statista in collaboration with TIME, recognizing airports across the globe that excel in passenger experience and operational performance. The ranking draws on a broad survey of passengers across all continents rating their experience with up to five airports they have used in the past three years, conducted between July 27 and September 4, 2026, using an online access panel. These survey results are combined with an independent flight data analysis covering more than 30 million flights operated between July 2025 and June 2026, provided by OAG. Together, the two data sources provide a robust, data-driven foundation for comparing global airports on both the quality of the experience they deliver and the reliability of the flights they handle. Methodology The airport universe was compiled from a broad set of international airports for which sufficient data were available. Of these, airports handling at least one million passengers per year qualified for inclusion in the full evaluation, resulting in a final group of airports large enough to be assessed reliably on both passenger experience and operational performance. Airports were divided into four categories to allow better comparisons: • Major Airports: >= 50 million yearly passengers • Large Airports: 25 million to • Mid-sized Airports: 10 million to • Smaller Airports: Following the survey and operational-data assessment, 226 airports ultimately received a World’s Best Airports distinction. To be considered, an airport must meet the following criteria: • Passenger volume threshold: The airport must handle at least one million passengers per year, ensuring that only airports with a meaningful, globally relevant scale of operations are evaluated. • Data coverage: The airport must be covered by a sufficient number of passenger survey responses and by the operational flight-performance data to allow for a statistically reliable assessment. • Safety and quality control: As a final measure, a quality control review was conducted to screen for recent severe safety incidents. Any airport involved in critical safety violations or major accidents was excluded from the final ranking, ensuring that all recognized entities maintain high standards of operational safety. Building on this core universe, a number of further rankings highlight airports that stand out for particular size segments, regions, or service dimensions, such as transfer experience or family friendliness. These rankings draw on the same underlying survey and operational data but apply dimension-specific eligibility thresholds, so that each award reflects a sample that is meaningful for its respective category. Data sources and collection The ranking draws on two complementary data sources to ensure both passenger perspective and operational accuracy. Survey data: Statista conducted a global survey among passengers, collecting their experiences with airports they have used in the past three years. Participants could freely evaluate airports, supported by an auto-complete function, and rated their satisfaction with various dimensions of the airport experience, such as wayfinding and orientation, security experience, baggage handling, cleanliness, connectivity, airport facilities, lounges, family friendliness, and transit experience, as well as their overall satisfaction and likelihood to recommend the airport to others. The survey was conducted in the following countries: • Australia • Brazil • Canada • China • France • Germany • Italy • Japan • South Africa • South Korea • Spain • Sweden • Switzerland • The Netherlands • United Kingdom • United States Flight data: Operational performance data for more than 30 million flights was provided by OAG, covering punctuality, cancellation rates, flight destinations, and passenger volumes for the period from July 2025 to June 2026. This data complements the survey results with an independent, fact-based measure of how reliably flights through each airport operate. Scoring model The ranking combines passenger survey results with operational performance data into a single assessment for each airport. Passenger experience: This component reflects travelers’ direct assessment of their experience at the airport, combining their overall satisfaction with an airport and their willingness to recommend it to others, as captured through the global survey. Operational reliability: This component is based on the independent operational flight data, capturing punctuality and the rate of cancellations recorded across all flights operated through the airport in the assessment period. An airport’s passenger volume is additionally factored into the final score on a logarithmically compressed scale. This reflects the principle of diminishing marginal returns to scale, ensuring that major hubs receive appropriate credit for the scale of passengers they serve, while preventing size alone from determining the outcome. As a result, a large airport cannot compensate for a weak passenger or reliability performance through scale alone, and a smaller airport with an excellent performance can still rank among the best. Airports that achieve a leading combined score receive the overall “World’s Best Airports” recognition. See the full lists. Disclaimer: The ranking is composed exclusively of airports that are eligible regarding the scope described in this document. A mention in the ranking is a positive recognition based on passenger evaluations and operational performance at the time. The ranking is the result of an elaborate process which, due to the interval of data collection and analysis, is a reflection of the assessment of the participants during the survey period. Furthermore, events preceding or following the period July 1, 2026 to October 2, 2026, and/or pertaining to individual persons affiliated/associated to the airports were not included. As such, the results of this ranking should not be used as the sole source of information for future deliberations. The information provided in this ranking should be considered in conjunction with other available information about airports. The quality of airports that are not included in the ranking is not disputed.

items.originalTitle: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now one light-day away
items.author: Jess Weatherbed
items.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe is now one light-day away
items.summary: Voyager 1 has traveled further than any other man-made object. | Photo by NASA/Hulton Archive/Getty Images After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: the spacecraft is now officially one light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, "very, very far." The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET, and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet - equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours. It's the furthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1's journey isn't over yet. It's been heading towards a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.originalTitle: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy
items.author: Leah Harper
items.title: ‘I hope paramedics are on standby for the sex scenes!’ The wet and wild TV experience leaving fans dizzy
items.summary: From icy squirts to bed-bouncing vibrations, erotic hockey drama Heated Rivalry just got even raunchier in ‘extreme sensory’ 4DX cinema screenings. But one scene proved too much – even for the super fans I’m in the cinema foyer when I first spot them: hockey jerseys. Lots of them. “I’ve no idea what to expect!” giggles Chloe, who is wearing a black and yellow “Rozanov” jersey. Like me, she has never been to a 4DX screening before – but when Cineworld announced it would be showing episodes five and six of queer hockey drama Heated Rivalry in the novel format, she booked tickets immediately. “I actually had tickets for the 2D screening, but cancelled them for this,” she says. Over the last two weeks, Heated Rivalry fans have been treated to big screen marathons of Jacob Tierney’s hit TV show, based on Rachel Reid’s bestselling book series, Game Changers. But 4DX is next level. The “extreme sensory” cinema technology is usually deployed for high-octane action flicks – films with epic battles or chase sequences. Still, with Cineworld offering the opportunity to “immerse yourself in the motion, wind, water [and] scent” of major league hockey’s raunchiest fictional romance, who could resist?

items.originalTitle: Reid Wiseman, the astronaut shooting for the moon in F1 with Mercedes
items.author: Giles Richards in Las Vegas
items.title: Reid Wiseman, the astronaut shooting for the moon in F1 with Mercedes
items.summary: Nasa crew member is fast seeing the similarities between flying Artemis into lunar orbit and the F1 team’s drive for sporting brilliance There are characters aplenty within Formula One, a sport that attracts the larger-than-life, and at the sharp end can be a parade ground for swaggering egos. Yet the newest addition to the paddock is a man whose quietly spoken, understated thoughtfulness and insight is compelling. Now part of the Mercedes team, Reid Wiseman has been to the moon and with it brings a perspective like no other. Wiseman was one of four astronauts, alongside Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, who completed the Artemis II lunar flyby in April. Last month Wiseman, the mission’s commander, became an ambassador for Mercedes’ F1 team, formalising a relationship that had been growing over several years, to the delight of his daughter Katey, a fan of newly crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli.
